passages.t: Why does the Almighty not set times for judgment?
passages.happening:
“Why does the Almighty not reserve times for judgment? Why may those who know Him never see His days?” (verse 1).

Men move boundary stones and pasture stolen flocks. ‘They drive away the donkey of the fatherless and take the widow’s ox in pledge’ (verse 3). They push the needy off the road. The poor forage in the wasteland like wild donkeys and glean the vineyards of the wicked. They sleep naked in the cold and huddle against the rocks in the mountain rain. ‘The fatherless infant is snatched from the breast; the nursing child of the poor is seized for a debt’ (verse 9). They carry sheaves and go hungry, tread the winepresses and go thirsty.

“From the city, men groan, and the souls of the wounded cry out, yet God charges no one with wrongdoing” (verse 12).
passages.hearers:
In chapter 23 Job spoke of his own longing to find God. Here he steps back and looks at the whole social order, and he sees the same absence of justice everywhere. Eliphaz had accused Job of oppressing widows and orphans (22:6-9). Job answers, in effect, that such oppression is real and widespread, and that the oppressors are not being punished, which is the opposite of what Eliphaz's theology requires.

Most people in that world farmed small plots, the powerful controlled land and credit, and a bad harvest or a debt could push a family into destitution. Moving a boundary stone quietly seized a neighbor's land. Debt could cost a family its animals, its land and even its children, pledged or sold into servitude. Israel's law sought to limit all of this, and the prophets denounced it.

Gleaning, gathering what the harvesters left, was the right of the poor in Israel. Here it is their only way to live. The bitterest picture is of laborers who handle food all day and go hungry.

Verse 12 has a pointed echo. The word for wrongdoing is the word of 1:22, where Job did not charge God with wrongdoing. Now Job says that God charges no one.
passages.later: Israel's law forbade the first crime on Job's list: ‘You must not move your neighbor’s boundary marker, which was set up by your ancestors’ (Deuteronomy 19:14).
passages.asks: Job looked past his own pain to the poor around him. Ask who carries the harvest in your world and goes hungry. And ask what you could do about one of the wrongs Job names.

passages.happening: ‘Then there are those who rebel against the light, not knowing its ways or staying on its paths’ (verse 13). When daylight is gone, the murderer rises to kill the poor. The adulterer waits for twilight and covers his face, thinking no eye will see him. In the dark they dig through houses, and by day they shut themselves in. ‘For to them, deep darkness is their morning’ (verse 17).
passages.hearers:
The scene moves from the countryside to the city at night. Houses were usually built of mud brick, and a thief could dig through a wall rather than break down a door.

Job calls the murderer, the adulterer and the burglar rebels against the light. The word for rebel, marad, is often used of revolt against a king. Their crimes are a revolt against the order God has set in the world. The chapter shows sin in both its forms: the systems of debt and land that crush the poor, and private crimes hidden by darkness.
passages.later: The law speaks of the same night thief: ‘If a thief is caught breaking in and is beaten to death, no one shall be guilty of bloodshed’ (Exodus 22:2).
passages.asks: The wrongdoers in Job's picture loved the dark. Ask what you do that you would rather no one saw. And ask what it would mean to live in the light, with nothing to cover.

passages.happening:
The wicked are but foam on the surface of the water, and their share of the land is cursed. ‘As drought and heat consume the melting snow, so Sheol steals those who have sinned’ (verse 19). The womb forgets them and the worm feeds on them.

They prey on the childless and the widow. God gives them a sense of security, ‘but His eyes are on their ways’ (verse 23). They are lifted up for a moment, then gone, cut off like heads of grain.

“If this is not so, then who can prove me a liar and reduce my words to nothing?” (verse 25).
passages.hearers:
This last section seems to say what the friends have said, that the wicked vanish quickly. That is why it is one of the most debated passages in the book.

Verse 23 is important on any reading. Even when the wicked feel secure, God's eyes are on their ways.

Verse 25 ends Job's reply with a challenge. Let anyone show that what he has said about the world is false.
passages.hard:
Verses 18 to 24 seem to say the opposite of what Job has been arguing. Who is speaking?

The difficulty is real, and there is no agreement. In chapter 21 Job denied that the wicked are quickly punished, yet these verses picture them as foam on the water and grain cut off. One view is that the text has been disturbed and that these verses belong to one of the friends, since the third round is unusually short: Bildad speaks only six verses in chapter 25, and Zophar does not speak at all. A second keeps the verses with Job but reads them as his quotation of the friends' position, which he then challenges in verse 25. A third reads the verbs as wishes: may their portion be cursed, may Sheol take them, and several translations render them that way. A fourth takes them as Job's own view that the wicked do die in the end, but only as everyone dies, so that their end proves nothing.

Each reading has defenders, and these notes take no side. What is clear is that the chapter as a whole presses a question the friends cannot answer: why the Almighty does not set times for judgment that the faithful can see.
passages.asks: Job dared anyone to prove him wrong. Ask whether you are willing to look as honestly at the world as he did. And ask what you hope for when you pray for justice.
